title: Cap. II Arg. 5: 1 Tim. 2:4 — common will to save all grounds foresight-election
latin: Quinto, ex 1 Timoth. ii. 4. Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri, hunc in modum argumentantur, Deum ex hac communi voluntate salvandi omnes, dare omnibus sufficientem gratiam qua ad salutem perducantur. Quod itaque quosdam eligit ad gloriam, quosdam praeterit, id inde evenire, quod praevideat quosdam cooperaturos huic gratiae & in sanctitate perseveraturos, quosdam aut non omnino cooperaturos, aut in bonis operibus & fide non permansuros: Ergo nulla est electio ad gloriam nisi ex praescientia meritorum.
pass_a: Fifth, from 1 Tim. ii. 4. God wills all men to be saved, they argue in this way: that God, from this common will of saving all, gives to all sufficient grace by which they may be led to salvation. That therefore he elects some to glory and passes by others comes to pass because he foresees that some will cooperate with this grace and persevere in holiness, but others either will not cooperate at all, or will not remain in good works and faith: Therefore there is no election to glory except from foresight of merits.
pass_b: Fifth: from 1 Timothy 2:4 — "God wills all men to be saved" — they argue that from this common will to save all, God gives everyone sufficient grace to reach salvation. So some are elect to glory and others passed by only because he foresaw who would cooperate with that grace and persevere in holiness, and who would not cooperate at all, or would not remain in good works and faith. Therefore, they say, there is no election to glory except from foresight of merits.

lemmas.gloss: God wills all men to be saved
common will to save all as their starting point
election allegedly from foresight of cooperation / perseverance

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 5: will to save tied to will to teach — God did not teach all
latin: Voluntas haec Divina de salute omnium hominum, non aliter concipienda, quam illa quae conjungitur de eruditione omnium hominum. Connectuntur enim ab Apostolo; Deus vult omnes salvos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Est autem certissimum, tum ex verbo Dei, tum ex ipso eventu, Deum non habuisse aut habere voluntatem erudiendi omnes, sive perducendi omnes singulatim ad salutiferae veritatis cognitionem: Rom. x. 14. Quomodo invocabunt eum in quem non crediderint? quomodo autem credent ei de quo non audierint? quomodo audient absque praedicante? aut quomodo praedicabunt si non mittantur? At Deus praeteritis generationibus dimisit omnes gentes suis ipsarum viis incedere; Act. xiv. 16. Ac veritatis agnitionem soli nationi Judaeorum concessit. Post Christi adventum lux veritatis non statim omnibus ex voluntate Dei affulsit. Ad tempus prohibiti sunt Apostoli in viam gentium abire, Matth. x. 5. Aliquanto post vetiti sunt etiam ne praedicarent verbum in Asia, Actor. xvi. 6. Atque ut ad nostra secula descendamus, quot nationes in Novo orbe detectas habemus, ad quas salutiferae veritatis per multa secula ne tenuissima quidem aura pervenit? An dici potest Deus voluisse illos ad agnitionem veritatis venire, ad quos noluit praecones veritatis mittere? Videte Prosperum Aquitanicum, ad Capit. Gall. Respons. 4. & Sent. 4. Si itaque sic intelligunt verba Apostoli, ut sentiant Deum, quantum in se est, velle omnes & singulos mortales in Adamo lapsos propter Christum donare salutiferae veritatis cognitione & ipsa salute, aut in hac illorum sententia manifestum errorem, aut in Divina voluntate manifestam infirmitatem agnoscere est necesse; nam volens potens operatur.
pass_a: This Divine will concerning the salvation of all men is not to be conceived otherwise than that which is joined concerning the instructing of all men. For they are connected by the Apostle: God wills all to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth. But it is most certain, both from the word of God and from the event itself, that God has not had and does not have a will of instructing all, or of leading all one by one to the knowledge of saving truth: Romans x. 14. How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? or how shall they preach unless they be sent? But God in past generations suffered all nations to walk in their own ways; Acts xiv. 16. And he granted the knowledge of the truth to the Jewish nation alone. After the coming of Christ the light of truth did not at once shine upon all by the will of God. For a time the Apostles were forbidden to go into the way of the Gentiles, Matthew x. 5. A little later they were also forbidden to preach the word in Asia, Acts xvi. 6. And to come down to our own ages, how many nations detected in the New World do we have, to whom through many ages not even the slightest breath of saving truth has reached? Can it be said that God willed those to come to the knowledge of the truth to whom he was unwilling to send heralds of the truth? See Prosper of Aquitaine, on the Chapters of the Gauls, Response 4 and Sentence 4. If therefore they so understand the Apostle's words that they think God, as far as in him lies, wills to give to all and each of the mortals fallen in Adam, for Christ's sake, the knowledge of saving truth and salvation itself, it is necessary either to acknowledge a manifest error in this opinion of theirs, or a manifest weakness in the Divine will; for he who wills, being able, works.
pass_b: This divine will for the salvation of all men must be read with the will joined to it — the will to teach all men. Paul binds them: God wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4). Yet it is certain from God's word and from history that he has not willed to teach all, or to lead every person one by one to saving truth. Romans 10:14: how will they call on him in whom they have not believed? how believe without hearing? how hear without a preacher? how preach unless they are sent? In past generations God let the nations walk in their own ways (Acts 14:16) and gave knowledge of the truth to Israel alone. After Christ's coming the light did not at once shine on all by his will: for a time the apostles were barred from the Gentile road (Matthew 10:5), and later forbidden to preach in Asia (Acts 16:6). Come to our own age: how many nations found in the New World have for centuries not felt even a breath of saving truth? Can God be said to have willed them to know the truth when he would not send them heralds of it? See Prosper of Aquitaine on the Gallic chapters (Response 4 and Sentence 4). If they take Paul to mean that God, as far as in him lies, wills to give every fallen child of Adam saving knowledge and salvation itself for Christ's sake, you must either call their reading a clear error or confess weakness in the divine will — for the one who wills, and can, acts.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 5: ancestor-covenant dodge refuted — Adam ok, Indian via grandparents not
latin: Sed nonnulli, ut tueantur hanc sententiam, urgent Deum per omnia secula voluisse omnes singulatim ad veritatis cognitionem venire, & salvos fieri, quatenus in foedere Dei comprehendebantur, non vero quatenus ab illo foedere in se, aut in parentibus exciderant: Vocasse etiam Deum universos ad veritatis agnitionem, vel in sua persona, vel saltem in persona parentum, avorum, abavorum, &c. Sed hoc commento nihil stultius. Nam primo, qui ob aliquam causam antecedentem decrevit, antequam nascerentur, innumeras singulares personas ad veritatis agnitionem nunquam vocare, is non habuit voluntatem vocandi hasce easdem singulatim. Dein, quam a sensu communi alienum est, Deum vocare voluisse hanc singularem personam ad cognitionem salutiferae veritatis in persona avorum aut abavorum suorum? Haeccine est illa universalis & sufficiens gratia ex qua probant Deum velle omnium salutem sigillatim? An quilibet ex majoribus una persona esse praesumitur cum suis nepotibus? Aut Deus ideo nepoti aliquid dare voluisse dicetur sigillatim & personaliter, quia id dederit impiis & ingratis avis ejus aut abavis qui illud rejecerunt? Qui hoc sensu sufficientem gratiam & generalem Dei voluntatem quoad omnium salutem velit defendere, non ad avos aut abavos, sed ad primum parentem humani generis se recipere debet. Nam in Adamo, qui fuit radix, & sustinuit quasi communem personam humani generis, non incommode dicere possumus, Deum voluisse salutem omnium: Sed dicere Deum sigillatim voluisse salutem hujus Indi aut Americani, atque insuper voluisse ut is ad veritatis salutiferae cognitionem sufficienter vocaretur, cui nunquam misit praeconem aliquem gratiae salutiferae, nec alia ratione id asserere quam quod avus ejus aut abavus, aut quisquis tandem ille fuerit majorum ejus, quingentis aut mille fortasse abhinc annis sua culpa Evangelium rejecit, & hoc suo facto posteros a gratiae foedere exclusit, hoc, inquam, tueri, est ejus qui nihil aliud habet quod dicat; refellere autem illius, qui nihil aliud habet quod agat.
pass_a: But some, to defend this opinion, urge that God through all ages willed all one by one to come to the knowledge of the truth and to be saved, insofar as they were comprehended in God's covenant, but not insofar as they had fallen from that covenant in themselves or in their parents: and that God also called all to the knowledge of the truth, either in their own person, or at least in the person of parents, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, etc. But nothing is more foolish than this fiction. For first, he who for some antecedent cause decreed, before they were born, never to call countless singular persons to the knowledge of the truth, did not have a will of calling these same ones one by one. Next, how alien from common sense is it that God should have willed to call this singular person to the knowledge of saving truth in the person of his grandfathers or great-grandfathers? Is this that universal and sufficient grace from which they prove God wills the salvation of all seal by seal? Is each of the ancestors presumed to be one person with his grandchildren? Or will God be said to have willed to give something to a grandson seal by seal and personally because he gave it to that grandson's impious and ungrateful grandfathers or great-grandfathers who rejected it? Whoever wishes to defend sufficient grace and God's general will as to the salvation of all in this sense ought to take refuge not in grandfathers or great-grandfathers, but in the first parent of the human race. For in Adam, who was the root and sustained as it were the common person of the human race, we can not inconveniently say that God willed the salvation of all: But to say that God seal by seal willed the salvation of this Indian or American, and moreover willed that he should be sufficiently called to the knowledge of saving truth, to whom he never sent any herald of saving grace, and to assert it on no other ground than that his grandfather or great-grandfather, or whoever of his ancestors it finally was, five hundred or perhaps a thousand years ago by his own fault rejected the Gospel, and by this act of his excluded his posterity from the covenant of grace — this, I say, to defend is the part of one who has nothing else to say; but to refute it is the part of one who has nothing else to do.
pass_b: Some, to save the opinion, press that through every age God willed each person to come to truth and be saved insofar as they stood in his covenant, not insofar as they fell from it in themselves or in their parents — and that he called everyone to the truth either in their own person or at least in parents, grandparents, and great-grandparents. Nothing is more foolish. First: if for some prior cause God decreed, before they were born, never to call countless particular persons to the truth, he did not will to call those same people one by one. Next: how far from common sense is it that God called this one person to saving truth in the person of his grandparents? Is that the universal sufficient grace by which they prove he wills everyone's salvation person by person? Is each ancestor one person with his grandchildren? Or did God will to give something personally to a grandson because he once gave it to impious grandparents who threw it away? Anyone who wants to defend sufficient grace and a general will to save all this way should go not to grandparents but to the first parent of the race. In Adam — the root, the common person of humankind — we may fairly say God willed the salvation of all. But to say he personally willed the salvation of this Indian or American, and that he was sufficiently called to saving truth, though God never sent him a herald of saving grace — and to rest that only on some ancestor five hundred or a thousand years ago who by his own fault rejected the Gospel and cut his line out of the covenant of grace — that defense belongs to someone with nothing left to say; refuting it belongs to someone with nothing better to do.

lemmas.gloss: singular Native call via ancestors rejected

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 5 Primo: salvos fieri vs facere — preceptive will, not decretive
latin: Verum si non placet haec sententia, quis tandem sensus verborum Apostoli? Primo, animadvertendum est, non dixisse Apostolum, Deus vult omnes homines salvos facere, & ad agnitionem veritatis efficacia praedicationis & Spiritus pertrahere; sed, vult omnes salvos fieri, & venire ad cognitionem veritatis. Nam Deo volenti salvum facere nullum hominum resistit arbitrium, ut vere Augustinus De corrept. & grat. cap. 14. Hisce igitur verbis exprimitur potius quid Deus velit ab hominibus fieri, quam quid velit in hominibus facere. Vult Deus, ut Ministri Evangelici teneantur, quantum in illis est, niti ut omnes salvi fiant, & ad Christum veniant; vult ut singuli Christiani orando, aliisque quibus possunt modis, promoveant salutem omnium hominum. Nostrum est, inquit Augustinus, qui nescimus quisnam pertineat ad numerum praedestinatorum, velle omnes salvos fieri, cap. 15. Ad voluntatem igitur praecipientem, quae homines dirigit, haec verba pertinent; non ad voluntatem decernentem, quae bonum homini destinatum infallibiliter largitur.
pass_a: But if this opinion does not please, what then is the sense of the Apostle's words? First, it must be noticed that the Apostle did not say, God wills to make all men saved, and to draw them to the knowledge of the truth by the efficacy of preaching and of the Spirit; but, he wills all to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For to God willing to make someone saved no human will resists, as Augustine truly says in De correptione et gratia chapter 14. By these words therefore is expressed rather what God wills to be done by men, than what he wills to do in men. God wills that Gospel ministers be bound, as far as in them lies, to strive that all may be saved and come to Christ; he wills that individual Christians by praying, and by other means they can, promote the salvation of all men. It is ours, says Augustine, who do not know who belongs to the number of the predestined, to will that all be saved, chapter 15. These words therefore pertain to the preceptive will, which directs men; not to the decretive will, which infallibly bestows the good destined for a man.
pass_b: If that reading fails, what do Paul's words mean? First notice: he did not say God wills to make all men saved and drag them to the truth by the force of preaching and the Spirit. He said he wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4). When God wills to make someone saved, no human will blocks him — so Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace 14. These words show what God wills people to do, more than what he wills to work inside them. He wills gospel ministers, as far as they can, to labor that all may be saved and come to Christ; he wills each Christian, by prayer and every means he can, to further the salvation of all. It is ours, Augustine says, who do not know who belongs to the number of the predestined, to will that all be saved (On Rebuke and Grace 15). So the text belongs to the preceptive will that directs us — not to the decretive will that infallibly gives the good God has destined for a person.

lemmas.gloss: no resist to making-saved; our duty to will all saved

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 5 Secundo: approbative vs effectual will — no singular sufficient grace from approval
latin: Secundo, notandum est Deum dici velle aliquid voluntate affectionis, vel voluntate effectus, ut distinguit Thomas, Quaest. Disp. De voluntate Dei, art. 1. vel ut alii loquuntur, Deus dicitur velle aliquid approbative, ut quod est in se bonum & amabile, vel efficaciter, ut quod decrevit propter gloriam suam in singulari aliquo subjecto efficere. Prior voluntas nihil aliud designat quam simplicem complacentiam Divinae voluntatis in re aliqua, tanquam Divinae naturae consentanea: Posterior denotat absolutum decretum communicandi hoc bonum singulariter alicui personae. Verbi causa, Castitas, Sapientia, Fides, Salus, sunt bona amabilia, & considerata in se Divinae voluntati consentanea: Recte igitur dicimus Deum velle ut omnes homines casti, sapientes, fideles, salvi fiant. Sed hoc intelligendum de voluntate approbante, quae tendit in rem secundum se consideratam, non de voluntate efficiente, quae statuit rem talem in tali persona operari. Frustra igitur ab illa priori voluntate, quae per se nihil decernit de singularibus personis, moliuntur illud deducere, Deum velle cuivis singulari personae concedere quod sufficit ad salutem ejus procurandam. Frustra etiam huic subnectunt, Deum ex praevisione quinam sint recte usuri hisce mediis, quinam minime, alios eligere ad salutem, alios praeterire & reprobare.
pass_a: Second, it must be noted that God is said to will something by a will of affection, or by a will of effect, as Thomas distinguishes in the Disputed Questions on the will of God, article 1; or as others speak, God is said to will something approbatively, as what is in itself good and lovable, or efficaciously, as what he has decreed for his own glory to effect in some singular subject. The former will designates nothing other than a simple complacency of the Divine will in some thing, as agreeable to the Divine nature: the latter denotes an absolute decree of communicating this good singularly to some person. For example, Chastity, Wisdom, Faith, Salvation are lovable goods, and considered in themselves agreeable to the Divine will: rightly therefore we say that God wills that all men be chaste, wise, faithful, saved. But this is to be understood of the approving will, which tends toward the thing considered according to itself, not of the effecting will, which decides to work such a thing in such a person. In vain therefore from that former will, which of itself decrees nothing concerning singular persons, do they strive to deduce that God wills to grant to any singular person whatever suffices for procuring his salvation. In vain also do they attach to this that God, from foresight of who will use these means rightly and who least, elects some to salvation and passes by and reprobates others.
pass_b: Second: God is said to will something by a will of affection or of effect — so Thomas in the Disputed Questions on the will of God, art. 1 — or, as others put it, approbatively (what is good and lovable in itself) or efficaciously (what he has decreed to work for his glory in some particular person). The first is only the divine will's simple delight in a thing as fitting God's nature; the second is an absolute decree to give that good to someone in particular. Chastity, wisdom, faith, salvation are lovable goods, and in themselves agreeable to God's will — so we rightly say God wills all people to be chaste, wise, faithful, and saved. Hear that of the approving will, which looks at the thing as such, not of the effecting will, which decides to work it in this or that person. From that prior will — which of itself settles nothing about particular persons — they cannot force the claim that God wills to grant each person whatever suffices for his salvation. Still less can they hang on it that, from foresight of who will use those means well and who will not, he elects some to salvation and passes by and reprobates others.

lemmas.gloss: approve good-in-itself vs decree in a subject
foresight of use of means cannot hitch to mere approval

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 5 close: Augustine / Gregory / Aquinas — all = kinds, not foresight-cooperation
latin: Postremo, si quis obstinate contendat verba Apostoli de efficaci voluntate Dei esse intelligenda, is nunquam se expediet, si aliter locum capiat quam ab Augustino, Gregorio & Scholasticis olim fuit explicatus. Sic Augustinus de corrept. & grat. cap. 14. Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri, ut intelligantur omnes praedestinati, quia omne genus hominum est in iis. Et Gregorius, Omnes homines vult salvos fieri, quia ex omni hominum genere eligit, quos ad gaudium aeternae salutis trahit. In 1. Reg. lib. 5. cap. 4. Aquinas denique in Commentariis ad haec ipsa verba, Est distributio pro generibus singulorum, non pro singulis generum. Quandoquidem ergo hic locus non probat Deum voluntate beneplaciti velle salutem omnium & singulorum, multo minus probat Deum eligere homines ad salutem ex praescientia futurae cooperationis, qua se accommodent huic voluntati Dei.
pass_a: Finally, if anyone stubbornly contends that the Apostle's words are to be understood of God's efficacious will, he will never extricate himself if he takes the place otherwise than it was formerly explained by Augustine, Gregory, and the Scholastics. So Augustine in De correptione et gratia chapter 14: God wills all men to be saved, that all the predestined be understood, because every kind of men is in them. And Gregory: He wills all men to be saved, because from every kind of men he elects those whom he draws to the joy of eternal salvation. On 1 Kings book 5 chapter 4. Aquinas finally in the Commentaries on these very words: It is a distribution for the kinds of individuals, not for the individuals of the kinds. Since therefore this place does not prove that God by the will of good pleasure wills the salvation of all and each, much less does it prove that God elects men to salvation from foresight of future cooperation by which they accommodate themselves to this will of God.
pass_b: Last: if someone still insists Paul's words mean God's efficacious will, he will never get free unless he reads the place as Augustine, Gregory, and the scholastics long did. Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace 14: "God wills all men to be saved" — understand all the predestined, because every kind of human being is among them. Gregory: he wills all men to be saved because from every kind of people he elects those he draws to the joy of eternal salvation (on 1 Kings, book 5, ch. 4). Aquinas on the same words: the distribution is for the kinds of individuals, not for the individuals of the kinds. So this text does not prove that by the will of good pleasure God wills the salvation of every single person — and far less that he elects people to salvation from foresight of the future cooperation by which they would fit themselves to that will.

lemmas.gloss: Augustine: all = predestined containing every kind
Aquinas: kinds of individuals, not individuals of kinds
